back: An estimator is a function of the random data (a recipe, itself a random variable); an estimate is its value on one data set.

front: Bias and variance of an estimator
back: $\text{bias}=\mathbb E[\hat\theta]-\theta$; $\text{Var}=\mathbb E[(\hat\theta-\mathbb E\hat\theta)^2]$. Expected squared error $=\text{bias}^2+\text{Var}$.

front: Standard error of the sample mean
back: $\sigma/\sqrt N$. Four times the data halves the error bar.
$s^2=\frac1{N-1}\sum(x_n-\bar x)^2$. Dividing by $N$ gives $\mathbb E=\frac{N-1}{N}\sigma^2$, biased low.
$L(\theta)=-\sum_n\log p(y_n\mid x_n,\theta)$. Logs turn the product over examples into a sum; minus turns maximising into minimising.

front: Why does Gaussian noise give least squares?
back: $-\log$ of $\mathcal N(y\mid x^\top\theta,\sigma^2)$ is $\frac{(y-x^\top\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2}$ plus a constant in $\theta$, so the NLL is a scaled sum of squared errors.
$\arg\min_\theta[-\log p(x\mid\theta)-\log p(\theta)]$: maximise the posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\times$ prior; $p(x)$ is ignored.
Prior $\theta\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2I)$ with noise $\sigma^2$ gives ridge with $\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2$ (Bishop: $\lambda=\alpha/\beta$). A Laplace prior gives L1.
$P(\text{statistic at least this extreme}\mid H_0)$. It is not $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$ and not an effect size.

front: Correct reading of a 95% confidence interval
back: The procedure captures the true value in 95% of repeated experiments; one computed interval either contains it or not.
$m$ independent tests at level $\alpha$ give $1-(1-\alpha)^m$ chance of a false positive ($0.64$ for $m=20$). Bonferroni: test at $\alpha/m$.

front: Paired t statistic for model comparison
back: With fold differences $d_i$: $t=\bar d/(s_d/\sqrt K)$, $K-1$ degrees of freedom. Folds share training data so it is somewhat optimistic.
Resample the data with replacement $B$ times, recompute the statistic, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. No distribution formula needed.
With huge $N$ a trivial difference gets a tiny p-value. Report an effect size (difference in metric units, Cohen's $d$) alongside it.
$\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/N}$; for $\hat p=0.87$, $N=500$ it is $0.015$, so a 95% interval is about $\pm0.03$.
